sections.title: Introduction
rules: Maximum likelihood considers model parameters as unknown constant values.
Bayesian estimation considers model parameters as random variables.
We describe our initial belief about a parameter with a prior probability distribution.
The sample likelihood shows how likely the data is for a specific parameter value.
Bayes' rule combines the prior probability distribution and the sample likelihood.
This combination calculates the posterior probability distribution.
The marginal likelihood normalizes the posterior distribution so it integrates to one.
For a new input, the predictive distribution integrates over all parameter values.
We weight each parameter prediction by its posterior probability.
A generative graphical model shows how the parameter generates the data.
The past sample and a new instance are conditionally independent given the parameter.
Full Bayesian integration is frequently difficult to compute.
The Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) method selects the mode of the posterior distribution.
The MAP estimate assumes the posterior distribution has a narrow peak.
If the prior distribution is uniform, the MAP estimate equals the maximum likelihood estimate.

sections.title: Estimating the Parameter of a Distribution
rules: Discrete variables: We model multinomial data with discrete state probabilities.
The conjugate prior for a multinomial distribution is the Dirichlet distribution.
A conjugate prior produces a posterior distribution from the same probability family.
Hyperparameters represent imaginary sample counts before we observe actual data.
The posterior distribution adds observed sample counts to prior hyperparameters.
Larger hyperparameter values indicate higher confidence in the prior belief.
For binary data, the multinomial model becomes a Bernoulli distribution.
The conjugate prior for a Bernoulli distribution is the Beta distribution.
As the sample size increases, the posterior variance decreases.
Continuous variables: We estimate the mean and variance of a Gaussian distribution.
The conjugate prior for a Gaussian mean is another Gaussian distribution.
The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean.
The weights depend inversely on the variances of the prior and the sample.
If the sample size is large, the posterior mean approaches the sample mean.
If prior variance is small, the prior mean dominates the estimate.
The posterior variance is smaller than both the prior variance and the sample variance.
For unknown variance, we calculate precision as the reciprocal of variance.
The conjugate prior for Gaussian precision is the Gamma distribution.
The posterior Gamma distribution updates prior hyperparameters with sample statistics.

sections.title: Bayesian Estimation of the Parameters of a Function
rules: Regression: In linear regression, we predict a continuous target from inputs.
The model assumes additive Gaussian noise with zero mean and known precision.
Maximum likelihood minimizes the sum of squared errors between predictions and targets.
The Bayesian approach defines a zero-mean Gaussian prior distribution on weight parameters.
This Gaussian prior assumes weights stay close to zero.
The posterior distribution of the weights is also a Gaussian distribution.
The MAP estimate adds a regularization term to the diagonal of the input matrix.
This regularization is identical to ridge regression and weight decay in neural networks.
Ridge regression reduces weight magnitudes, but does not set weights to zero.
To select features, we replace the Gaussian prior with a Laplacian prior.
A Laplacian prior uses the L1 norm instead of the L2 norm.
The MAP estimate with a Laplacian prior is called the lasso.
The lasso sets redundant weights to zero and produces sparse models.
Basis and kernel functions: We map input vectors into high-dimensional feature spaces.
The dual representation expresses predictions directly as weighted sums of training instances.
A kernel function calculates inner products without computing explicit basis transformations.
Bayesian classification: We use a sigmoid function for two-class logistic discrimination.
The posterior distribution over weights is not Gaussian.
We use the Laplace approximation to fit a Gaussian distribution at the posterior mode.
The covariance matrix is the inverse of the Hessian matrix of second derivatives.
The probit function allows analytical integration for class predictions.

sections.title: Gaussian Processes
rules: A Gaussian process defines a prior probability distribution directly over functions.
Any finite collection of function values has a joint multivariate Gaussian distribution.
The mean function is usually set to zero.
The covariance matrix measures similarity between input points through a kernel function.
Common covariance functions include linear, polynomial, and Gaussian radial basis functions.
Observed outputs add Gaussian noise to the underlying function values.
The joint distribution of training targets and a new test point is Gaussian.
Conditioning on training data yields a Gaussian predictive distribution for the new point.
The predictive mean gives the point prediction as a weighted sum of kernel values.
The predictive variance indicates uncertainty at the query point.
Predictive variance is high in regions with few training examples.
Gaussian processes do not calculate explicit model parameters.
Training requires inverting an N-by-N covariance matrix.
Matrix inversion requires cubic computational time in the number of training examples.
For classification, we pass the Gaussian process output through a sigmoid function.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Bayesian methods provide a formal mathematical framework for Occam's razor.
Bayesian algorithms prefer simpler models that explain the observed data.
Critics note that subjective choice of prior distributions can introduce bias.
Modern computational power and Markov chain Monte Carlo make complex Bayesian inference practical.
Type 2 maximum likelihood optimizes hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood.
